ARES – Advanced Rover & Astronaut Exploration System

ARES is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning platform designed to support astronauts during future surface exploration missions. Developed as a web-based application, it integrates NASA Mars Trek mapping layers, including optical imagery, topographic data, thermal information and mineralogical context, within an interactive map focused on Jezero Crater.

The platform allows users to explore potential scientific targets, mark research locations, plan exploration routes, identify potential hazards, and organise Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). It also provides mission-planning tools, field notes, data visualisation and exportable mission information.

ARES addresses the challenge by bringing multiple types of planetary data and exploration-planning features into one accessible interface. It demonstrates how scientific information can support route planning, research decisions and astronaut awareness during Mars surface operations.

Its importance lies in helping make future human exploration more informed, organised and efficient. By connecting planetary science with practical mission-planning concepts, ARES offers an educational prototype of how astronauts and mission teams could interact with Martian terrain data when preparing for exploration.
details:
ARES – Advanced Rover & Astronaut Exploration System

ARES is a web-based Mars exploration and mission-planning platform developed to demonstrate how astronauts and mission teams could use scientific data to prepare for surface exploration on Mars. The application focuses on Jezero Crater, the landing region of NASA's Perseverance rover, and combines planetary mapping, scientific research and mission-planning tools in one interactive interface.

How It Works

ARES uses an interactive Mars map that incorporates NASA Mars Trek datasets, including optical imagery, MOLA topographic information, thermal inertia, surface roughness and mineralogical layers. Users can switch between available map layers, explore locations, mark scientific research targets, add field notes, identify potential hazards and draw proposed exploration routes. The platform also includes route-distance calculations, mission-planning tools, EVA time estimation, terrain-profile analysis using imported data, and options to export route information in GeoJSON and CSV formats.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ARES helps users understand how different types of planetary data can contribute to exploration decisions. It brings scientific research, geographical awareness and mission organisation together, demonstrating how astronauts could identify areas of interest, plan activities and consider potential terrain-related risks. Its intended impact is to encourage safer, more informed and better-organised approaches to future human exploration of Mars.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet.js for interactive mapping. NASA Mars Trek provides several planetary data layers, while USGS planetary mapping resources, NASA's Perseverance image archive and other NASA scientific resources support research and context. GeoJSON and CSV are used for importing and exporting mission information. The application is designed to run in a standard web browser without specialised hardware.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of ARES is its integration of planetary science and practical mission-planning concepts into a single interface. Instead of presenting Mars data as separate scientific resources, it gives users tools to interact with the information, annotate locations and develop their own exploration plans. It also distinguishes between verified scientific datasets and illustrative user-created annotations, avoiding the presentation of simulated information as actual scientific measurements.

Factors Considered by the Team

Our team considered scientific accuracy, data reliability, astronaut awareness, terrain conditions, route accessibility, mission time constraints, usability and the limitations of available datasets. We also considered the importance of making the platform accessible, understandable and useful for both scientific exploration and educational purposes. ARES is an educational prototype rather than a certified navigation or astronaut safety system; its routes and hazard annotations require further validation before any real mission use.
